orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the March 31, 2016 denial of summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on a foreign substance on the floor of defendant-owned premises on October 8, 2012. The substance and premises use are not specified in the opinion.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant’s submissions established noncreation prima facie. The overall dismissal motion nevertheless failed on constructive notice and causal-identification grounds; no final liability finding followed.
Defendant established lack of actual notice prima facie, separately from its unsuccessful constructive-notice showing.
Defendant failed to eliminate triable issues about constructive notice. The court does not identify particular evidence deficiencies, a hazard duration or a conclusive finding of notice.

Defendant failed to establish that identifying the cause would require speculation. The court explains that admissible proof other than plaintiff’s personal knowledge can establish cause; it does not identify that proof or finally find causation here.

quality.notes: Actual premises ownership is explicit. Defendant’s laundromat name alone does not establish the use of these premises, and no injured role is stated. Foreign substance is other, without inferring water, detergent or grease. Successful noncreation/actual-notice showings must remain distinct from failed constructive-notice and causation showings. No evidence formats are identified; the generic reference to other admissible proof does not justify adding a witness or record type. Source wording his or fall is preserved literally in the quoted continuation. All appealed relief is affirmed despite differing reasoning on individual grounds.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
On October 8, 2012, the plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell due to the presence of a foreign substance on the floor of premises owned by the defendant.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Molia, J.), dated March 31, 2016, which denied its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, although the evidence submitted in support of the defendant's motion demonstrated, prima facie, that it did not create or have actual notice of the alleged condition, its submissions failed to eliminate all triable issues of fact as to whether it had constructive notice of the alleged condition
Further, the defendant failed to establish, prima facie, that the cause of the plaintiff's fall cannot be identified without engaging in speculation
Rather, it means only that a plaintiff's inability to establish the cause of his or fall—whether by personal knowledge or by other admissible proof—is fatal to a cause of action based on negligence"

Inasmuch as the defendant failed to establish its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, the Supreme Court properly denied its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, regardless of the sufficiency of the opposition papers
We affirm.

orders.description: C&W’s limited appeal from the January 24, 2018 denial of dismissal of the amended complaint against it.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied C&W’s motion without prejudice to renewal after discovery.

facts.factual_summary: On June 23, 2011, plaintiff, a security guard employed by SEB, allegedly slipped on dirty water in a hallway leading to a loading dock in NYME’s Manhattan building. C&W managed the building and provided janitorial services; plaintiff described janitors washing trash cans with hoses in sinks in the loading dock area.

legal_issues.finding: C&W’s submission of plaintiff’s deposition, apart from procedural exhibits, did not establish noncreation prima facie. The court did not conclusively find that janitors produced the water; opposition sufficiency was immaterial.

evidence_discussed.description: C&W submitted plaintiff’s deposition transcript describing dirty hallway water and trash-can washing in the loading dock area; the transcript was insufficient to establish noncreation.
The motion also included copies of pleadings and an order concerning prior motions as exhibits; no specific substantive evidentiary value is attributed to these procedural materials.

quality.notes: The complete incident sentence is supported by separate exact quotes on either side of the artificial passage boundary. NYME owns the building, C&W manages it, and SEB is the employer (other); do not treat C&W as the owner or plaintiff’s employer. The accident was in the hallway leading to the loading dock, not expressly on the dock. Building use is unstated. Denial without prejudice to renewal after discovery is history; the appellate court actually decides failure of the noncreation showing, so the appeal is substantive. Third-party caption alone does not make this third-party-only. Generic notice standards do not establish separate notice rulings. No photographs, maintenance logs or janitor testimony are inferred.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.
On June 23, 2011, the plaintiff, who was a security guard employed by the defendant S.E.B.

Services of New York, Inc. (hereinafter SEB), for a building located in Manhattan which was owned by the defendant New York Mercantile Exchange, Inc. (hereinafter NYME), allegedly slipped and fell on water inside the building.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant Cushman & Wakefield, Inc., appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Kathy J. King, J.), dated January 24, 2018. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied that defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint insofar as asserted against it.
In June 2011, C&W managed the subject building, which included providing janitorial services.
The Supreme Court denied the motion without prejudice to renew after the completion of discovery.

Here, in support of its motion, besides providing copies of the pleadings and a copy of an order related to prior motions as exhibits, C&W only submitted a transcript of the plaintiff's deposition testimony.
The plaintiff testified that he slipped on dirty water as he traversed the hallway leading to the loading dock area, where janitors would wash trash cans inside large sinks with hoses.
Contrary to C&W's contention, the plaintiff's deposition testimony was insufficient to demonstrate, prima facie, that it did not create the alleged hazardous condition

Accordingly, we agree with the Supreme Court's determination to deny C&W's motion for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint insofar as asserted against it regardless of the sufficiency of the opposition papers

orders.description: Separate appeals by Waldbaum and Torneo from the July 21, 2009 order denying their respective dismissal motions.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on a puddle in the frozen food aisle of Waldbaum’s supermarket on the morning of August 31, 2005. Waldbaum owned and operated the store, and Torneo contracted to service its air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment; the puddle’s substance and source are not identified.

legal_issues.finding: Neither defendant established entitlement to judgment as a matter of law on constructive notice. Both motions were properly denied without examining opposition sufficiency; the opinion does not specify the deficient proof or establish notice as fact.

quality.notes: One appealed order resolves two motions and is fully affirmed on both appeals; multiple_orders=false. Owner/other/contractor captures Waldbaum’s owner/operator status and Torneo’s service role. The contract relationship is stated, but no submitted contract document or specific evidence format is identified. No independent contractor-duty doctrine, leak source, notice duration or actual-notice/creation determination is inferred from the general standard. Puddle is coded other because the liquid is unspecified. Plaintiff customer status is unstated. The 2005 accident date is explicit; eligibility follows the 2010 appellate decision date, not the accident year.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with one bill of costs.
On the morning of August 31, 2005, the plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell on a puddle in the frozen food aisle of a supermarket which was owned and operated by the defendant Waldbaum, Inc.

In a consolidated action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant Waldbaum, Inc., appeals from so much *936 of an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Emerson, J.), entered July 21, 2009, as denied its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it, and the defendant Torneo Mechanical Corporation separately appeals, as limited by its brief, from so much of the same order as denied its separate motion for the same relief.
At the time of the accident, the defendant Torneo Mechanical Corporation had a contract with Waldbaum, Inc., to service the air conditioning and refrigeration equipment in the store.
On the issue of constructive notice, neither defendant established its entitlement to judgment as a matter of law.
Under these circumstances it is unnecessary to consider the sufficiency of the plaintiffs opposition
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied both motions.
The Supreme Court denied the motions, and we affirm.

orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the March 25, 2020 denial of dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped in June 2016 at defendant’s residential building. At deposition she described an old, worn carpet patch on the fourth step of a staircase between the second and third floors.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant asserted lack of actual notice in the summary-judgment motion, but expressly did not pursue that argument on appeal. No appellate finding establishes or negates notice.
Defendant asserted lack of constructive notice in the summary-judgment motion, but expressly did not pursue that argument on appeal. No appellate finding establishes or negates notice.

Defendant failed to establish triviality as a matter of law. The photographs did not permit that determination, and his deposition also failed to establish it; the court did not finally decide the defect’s seriousness.

An unspecified remaining contention was improperly raised for the first time on appeal. Notice arguments were not pursued on appeal; no additional substantive topic is inferred from the unidentified contention.

Defendant also failed to establish that the carpet condition was not dangerous or defective. This initial-burden failure required denial without reviewing plaintiff’s opposition; it is not an affirmative liability finding.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s deposition described the worn carpet patch; defendant submitted his own deposition, which failed to establish absence of danger/defect or triviality.
Defendant submitted photographs of the staircase; the court found triviality could not be ascertained from them. They were discussed in the opinion, not independently inspected.

quality.notes: Residential ownership is explicit, but injured tenant/visitor role is unstated. Only June 2016 is supplied for the accident, so accident_date remains null; 2017 commencement and the 2020 order are different events. Carpet wear is other, without invented dimensions, elevation differential or structural stair defect. The 2022 decision date governs the preliminary validation period, not the 2023 correction date. Substantive dangerousness/triviality review makes the procedural argument ancillary. No notice finding follows from defendant’s choice not to argue notice. Unchanged initial rules applied without tuning to this validation-period case.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
In 2017, the plaintiff commenced this action to recover damages for personal injuries she allegedly sustained in June 2016 when she slipped and fell at a residential building owned by the defendant.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Carl J. Landicino, J.), dated March 25, 2020. The order denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

At her deposition, the plaintiff testified that, on the day at issue, she was descending a staircase between the second and third floors and slipped on an old, worn patch of carpet on the fourth step.

The defendant subsequently moved for summary judgment on the grounds that there was no defect on the steps, that any such defect was trivial, and therefore not actionable, and, in any event, that he lacked actual or constructive notice of same.
Here, the defendant failed to establish, prima facie, that the condition complained of was not dangerous or defective, or that it was trivial as a matter of law
In support of his motion, the defendant submitted, inter alia, his deposition testimony and photographs of the staircase at issue.
"[I]t is impossible to ascertain from the photographs submitted in support of the motion whether the alleged defective condition was trivial as a matter of law"

Moreover, the defendant's deposition testimony also failed to establish that the condition complained of was not defective or dangerous, or that it was trivial as a matter of law. We also note that on appeal the defendant does not argue that he lacked actual or constructive notice of the condition.

Since the defendant failed to meet his prima facie burden, the Supreme Court properly denied his motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint without regard to the sufficiency of the plaintiff's opposition
The defendant's remaining contention is improperly raised for the first time on appeal

orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the July 9, 2019 denial of summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped on a rug while walking through a restaurant owned and operated by defendant. The opinion does not describe a particular defect in the rug or its dimensions.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant established that the rug’s placement did not constitute a dangerous condition, and plaintiff raised no triable issue. Summary-judgment dismissal was therefore required.

quality.notes: Restaurant ownership and operation are explicit; owner/other represents both roles. Rug is other, without inferring an obstruction, fold or elevation difference. Plaintiff customer status and accident date are unstated. The holding concerns lack of a dangerous condition, not a separately stated open-and-obvious, trivial-defect or notice defense. No evidence format or expert proof is identified. Full reversal grants dismissal and favors defendant; dismissal is of the complaint, not the appeal.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously reversed on the law without costs, the motion is granted and the complaint is dismissed.
Memorandum: Plaintiff commenced this action seeking damages for injuries she sustained when she allegedly tripped and fell on a rug while walking through a restaurant owned and operated by defendant.
Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Erie County (Joseph R. Glownia, J.), entered July 9, 2019. The order denied the motion of defendant for summary judgment dismissing plaintiff's complaint.

Here, defendant established its entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by submitting evidence that the placement of the rug in the restaurant did not constitute a dangerous condition, and in opposition plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact
We therefore reverse the order, grant the motion, and dismiss the complaint.
We agree with defendant that Supreme Court erred in denying its motion seeking summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
